items.content_text:
Over 20,000 Chattanoogans came out last Saturday for the grand reopening of our beloved Walnut Street Bridge, and we can't stop thinking about it! This is not only one of Chattanooga's major connectors and historic landmarks, but a meeting place for the community.
 This major restoration wouldn't have been possible without the time and care of far too many people to name — from crew members who laid steel and wood to our community partners and business owners who adapted to the closures. This bridge is truly a testament of the compassion within our city, continuing to serve you all for another 136 years!
 Video by Bloom

There’s a lot of heart behind Chattanooga Floor Care.  

Matt Jeffery started the business with his dad more than 10 years ago. Now, as his dad begins to retire, Matt is carrying that business into its next chapter, taking what he learned from his dad and building on it.

Today, Chattanooga Floor Care turns existing concrete into unique, finished floors. The team works with each customer to find a solution that fits their space, needs, and vision.

As Matt looks toward what's next, the Chattanooga business community continues to play an important role. Through the Chattanooga Chamber, he's found new business, collaboration, and opportunities to connect with other business owners who want to see Chattanooga thrive.

We're proud to have Chattanooga Floor Care and Matt as a part of the Chamber community.

Year-on-year inflation in the OECD rose to 4.3% in August 2026, up from 4.1% in July.
 Headline inflation increased in 23 OECD countries, remained broadly stable in 12, and declined in only 3.
 Inflation remained well above the OECD average, at over 5.0%, in Colombia, Iceland, and Lithuania, and exceeded 30% in Türkiye.
 Learn more: https://brnw.ch/21x6eLM

**FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE**
 October 7, 2026
 Health and Social Services Division’s Violence Prevention Program Presents Second Annual “Healing Through Art” Event
 HAMILTON COUNTY, TN – The Hamilton County Health Department’s Violence Prevention Program, under the Health and Social Services Division, invites the community to its second annual Healing Through Art event on Saturday, October 10, 2026, at CommonSpirit Memorial Hospital. The free event is open to the public and brings together survivors, artists, community partners, and local organizations to highlight the role art can play in healing, recovery, and resilience. Through creative expression and community connection, Healing Through Art provides a supportive space for individuals to reflect, express emotions, and learn about resources available throughout the community. 
 This year’s event will feature keynote speakers, spoken art, and visual art from local artists for the first time. Attendees will also have the opportunity to purchase artwork directly from participating artists. A portion of each participating artwork purchase will be donated to either Partnership for Families, Children, and Adults or CommonSpirit Memorial Hospital, allowing attendees to support local artists while also giving back to organizations serving the community. 
 Attendees can expect:
 • Keynote speakers discussing the role of art in healing and resilience
 • Spoken art performances and visual art exhibits
 • Artwork available for purchase from participating artists
 • Community resources and information from local organizations and partners
 • Opportunities to connect with artists, survivors, advocates, and community members
 Event Details:
 • Date: October 10, 2026
 • Time: 11:00 a.m. – 2:00 p.m.
 • Location: CommonSpirit Memorial Hospital, Entrance B (Surgery Services) 
 o 2525 de Sales Avenue, Chattanooga, TN 37404
 “Healing Through Art reminds us that healing can take many forms, and sometimes expression begins where words end. By bringing survivors, artists, community partners, and residents together, we are creating a space where people can connect and find strength through creativity,” said Kamesha Green, Healthy & Safe Communities Program Manager at the Health Department. “This year, we are especially excited to give our community the opportunity to support the artists whose work tells these powerful stories while also giving back to organizations that provide critical support to survivors in our community.” 
 The Health Department thanks CommonSpirit Memorial Hospital, participating artists, and community partners for their support in making the second annual Healing Through Art event possible. For additional information or questions about the event, please contact Kamesha Green at KameshaG@HamiltonTN.gov. 
 Additional resources 
 • General Questions? Call the Health Department at 423-209-8000.
 • For Health Department information, visit: Health.HamiltonTN.org
 • To read this information in Spanish, visit the Health Department’s Spanish Facebook page at https://www.facebook.com/SaludHamiltonTN

items.content_text:
Friends,
 Many of you have reached out with questions about the plaques on the Walnut Street Bridge. Crews continue working daily to return each existing plaque to its original location following the renovation. It’s a long process with hundreds of plaques. 
 Prior to the renovation, several plaques were already missing. Efforts were made to locate those plaques through the original program, but unfortunately, they could not be recovered. To avoid leaving visible gaps, some of the remaining plaques were temporarily repositioned closer together.
 The organization that originally administered the plaque program, Friends of The Walnut Street Bridge, is no longer offering the program.
 As contracts are finalized and the necessary paperwork is completed, no additional features or plaques will be added to the bridge. This could take a good year. At this time, it is uncertain whether the non profit partner will bring back plaque program.

items.content_text:
Exploring Downtown: The Maclellan House 
 Tucked into the Bluff View Art District, the Maclellan House holds more than a century of Chattanooga history within its walls.
 Built in the late 1800s, the house was home to just two families: the Maclellans and, later, the Bryans. Many of the families’ original heirloom furnishings remain inside today, giving visitors a glimpse of what the home looked and felt like generations ago. 
 The house also has connections to Chattanooga’s broader history. Thomas Maclellan founded Provident Life & Accident Insurance Company, which later became part of Unum. His descendants later established the Maclellan Foundation, which continues its philanthropic work in Chattanooga today. 
 Today, the Maclellan House has been restored as a seven-room bed and breakfast. It was the oldest and last of Bluff View’s three historic inn homes to be restored, with much of the character and detail of the original residence still intact.
 More than a century after it was built, the Maclellan House offers a chance to step inside a piece of Chattanooga history that has been carefully preserved.

The International Bluegrass Music Association's World of Bluegrass is taking over Chattanooga October 20-24, filling our city with bluegrass through a multi-day conference, evening concerts across multiple venues, a weekend music festival, and an all-day community event: Pickin' in the Park. 
 Pickin' in the Park is a free, outdoor festival happening in the heart of downtown. It celebrates music, local artists, and our community.

 Plus, grab some food from local food trucks and shop arts & crafts vendors throughout the day.
 🌳 Open air
 🎟️ No tickets required
 🚧 No fencing

Commission Meeting Summary – October 5, 2026 
 Southern Adventist University MOU (Resolution 585): The commission approved a Memorandum of Understanding with Southern Adventist University. The city's partnership with SAU's School of Nursing began in 2025 with Storm Safety Day, and this MOU continues it. The agreement is needed mainly to cover liability for the event. 
 Airport Advisory Board Liaison (Resolution 586): The commission approved a motion to amend the resolution so the liaison's term ends in 2028 instead of 2027 and to appoint Vice Mayor Sadler as the commission's liaison to the Airport Advisory Board. 
 City Administration Report – 
 - Near Cambridge Square Development: Conversations are ongoing about a proposed development across from Cambridge Square. 
 - Railroad Crossing Cameras: Iron Rail Cams is reviewing the MOU for its crossing camera. 
 - Parks & Rec Board: The city is revising the Parks & Recreation Board ordinances. 
 - Library Ordinance: A library ordinance has been drafted as the city will take over library operations January 1, 2027. 
 - Free Community Shred Event: The event is next Tuesday, October 13th from 3 to 6 PM in the City Hall parking lot. 
 Commissioner Reports – 
 - Flock Cameras: Residents have been calling to ask whether the Flock cameras are still recording, and Commissioner Johnson deferred to the police chief. The chief confirmed the cameras are disconnected and no one has access to them. Flock has also acknowledged the city's notice of termination. To reassure residents, the commission has decided to cover the cameras with black trash bags, using Public Works' bucket truck until the cameras are removed by Flock. 
 - Rockslide Cleanup: Commissioner Johnson thanked Public Works for quickly clearing the large rocks that slid down the bank off Innovation Drive. Because the rocks damaged a fence, staff are meeting with a fence contractor about repairs. 
 - National Night Out: Commissioner Howse said she is looking forward to National Night Out. 
 Watch the full meeting: https://play.champds.com/collegedaletn/event/160

items.content_text:
AD | Waterfall hikes are my love language, and Visit Chattanooga is fluent 
 Chattanooga, Tennessee is America’s First National Park City and has been named one of the Best Adventure Towns in the US to Live and Play by National Geographic Adventure. After seeing this stunning waterfall, and all of the outdoor activities to enjoy, it’s easy to understand why!
 Middle Creek Falls is located just a few minutes outside of downtown Chattanooga and is one of the best swimming holes in the area. The trailhead is located along Suck Creek Road, and the hike is short at about 1.5 miles round tri. The trail does require some climbing over slippery rocks so wear sturdy shoes and take your time. Because of this, I wouldn’t recommend this hike for small children or anyone unsteady on their feet.
 The waterfall is around 20 feet tall with a lovely pool below that has a smooth floor, plus several other cascading areas and pools that give you plenty of options to enjoy while visiting!
 Always remember to leave no trace by staying on the trail, packing out all your trash, not carving into rocks or trees, and respecting other visitors while here!
 Have you visited Chattanooga yet and if so, what’s your favorite hike in the area?

items.content_text:
"Young people don't just want to be taught how to recycle, but rather they want ecosystems of engagement that combine personal action with structural power."

That was the message from our young peer research team to over 100 policymakers, politicians and practitioners from across youth and climate sectors at London's City Hall.

For the past two years, we've been mapping how London's green transition is being shaped by young people, and what could strengthen their voices. At the end of last month, the peer researchers shared findings from interviews across 18 London boroughs, kicking off a World Café guided by nine guest speakers.

We shared innovative tools and methods - from youth-led social action projects to policy co-design to political storytelling. We had frank conversations about the limits of current efforts, and about examples that inspired our research team. Together, we workshopped strategies for embedding youth participation in local administrations, and for building "ecosystems of engagement" that put young people at the centre of shaping a greener and more just future for their city.

Thank you to everyone who attended, to Partnership for Young London and Islington Council for co-delivering this project with LSE Cities, to the Greater London Authority for hosting us, and above all to the peer research team for making it all possible: Phool Ashraf, Cindy Boa; Jakaria Uddin; Maddy Westhead. 

Thanks also to our speakers: Cllr Rowena Champion, Isabella Tanner, Samia Dumbuya, Tim Alcroft, Pip Sayers, Stephanie F., Carlos Izsak, Martha Dillon, Bronwyn Hayward MNZM she/her, to Zoë Wilkins from the GLA, and to project coordinators Imogen Hamilton-Jones, Matthew Walsham, and Monika Milewska.

**FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE**
 October 5, 2026
 Hamilton County Health & Social Services, Erlanger Hospital, and Community Partners Unite to Encourage Vaccinations Ahead of Cold and Flu Season
 HAMILTON COUNTY, TN— Hamilton County Health & Social Services, Erlanger Hospital, and community partners are joining forces to encourage residents to protect themselves, their families, and the broader community by staying current on recommended and school-required vaccinations ahead of cold and flu season.
 Local health and medical leaders are reminding residents about the importance of vaccination and the community resources available to help families access potentially lifesaving vaccines.
 Respiratory illnesses such as influenza and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) circulate more widely during the fall and winter. Vaccination remains an important tool for reducing the risk of serious illness and protecting vulnerable community members. RSV can cause serious respiratory illness, particularly among infants, young children, and older adults.
 “In the pediatric ICU, we care for children who may have been healthy a week ago and now need help breathing. RSV and the flu can both have that effect on a baby or young child, and very quickly. Some may need oxygen, some may need a breathing tube, and some spend days in intensive care,” said Dr. Marvin Hall, Chief Medical Officer for the Children’s Hospital at Erlanger. “The Children's Hospital at Erlanger sees this each winter. We're coming together as a community now because the best time to protect a child is before these viruses start spreading. An RSV immunization and a flu shot this fall can keep many families out of the hospital.”
 Health officials also encourage parents and caregivers to review their children’s vaccination records and confirm that they are current on all school-required vaccines. Keeping children up to date helps protect individual students and reduce the spread of vaccine-preventable illnesses in schools, daycares, and the broader community.
 As part of this community-wide effort, the Hamilton County Health Department will participate in the statewide Fight Flu TN initiative by offering free flu shots to individuals ages six months and older on Tuesday, October 20, 2026.
 “Each year, we see firsthand how detrimental flu season can be to our community. It can mean missed days of school or work, increased visits to healthcare providers, and for some, serious illness & hospitalization,” said Dr. Stephen Miller, Health Officer for Hamilton County. “That is why Fight Flu TN is so vital. We must ensure everyone in our community has low-barrier access to potentially lifesaving vaccines. By making the flu shot free and easily accessible, we are giving more people the opportunity to protect themselves and our community.”
 Free flu shots will be available at: 
 Location – Adults and Children:
 • J.A. Henry Community YMCA:
 o 9:00 a.m. – 1:00 p.m.
 o 3500 Dodds Ave #108, Chattanooga, TN 37407
 • The Samaritan Center (The Health Department’s Mobile Unit)
 o 9:30 a.m. – 12:30 p.m.
 o 9231 Lee Hwy, Ooltewah, TN 37363
 Details:
 • No appointment or insurance is required.
 • Adults 18+ and children ages six months and older may participate.
 • Children’s vaccines are available at all flu vaccination event sites.
 • ONLY FREE THIS DAY – while supplies last.
 • Bilingual staff & an ASL interpreter will be on site(s).
 The flu vaccine is safe and effective. It can protect against common types of influenza and reduce the risk of the virus’s most serious symptoms and outcomes. Nationally, flu vaccination is estimated to have prevented approximately 10 million illnesses, 5 million medical visits, 180,000 hospitalizations, and 12,000 deaths during the 2024–2025 influenza season.
 Pregnant people, infants, older adults, and individuals with chronic medical conditions face a higher risk of severe flu complications. Flu symptoms may include coughing, fatigue, fever, headache, muscle aches, sore throat, and a stuffy or runny nose.
 For more information about precautions against respiratory viral illnesses, including influenza, visit the Tennessee Department of Health’s Respiratory Viral Illness webpage.
 Additional resources 
 • Questions? Call the Health Department at 423-209-8000.
 • Free interpretation services are available at all Health Department clinics. 
 • For Health Department information, visit: Health.HamiltonTN.org
 • To read this information in Spanish, visit the Health Department’s Spanish Facebook page at https://www.facebook.com/SaludHamiltonTN

It can mean missed days of school or work, increased visits to healthcare providers, and for some, serious illness & hospitalization,” said Dr. Stephen Miller, Health Officer for Hamilton County. “That is why Fight Flu TN is so vital. We must ensure everyone in our community has low-barrier access to potentially lifesaving vaccines. By making the flu shot free and easily accessible, we are giving more people the opportunity to protect themselves and our community.”
Free flu shots will be available at:
Location – Adults and Children:
• J.A. Henry Community YMCA:
o 9:00 a.m. – 1:00 p.m.
o 3500 Dodds Ave #108, Chattanooga, TN 37407
• The Samaritan Center (The Health Department’s Mobile Unit)
o 9:30 a.m. – 12:30 p.m.
o 9231 Lee Hwy, Ooltewah, TN 37363

• No appointment or insurance is required.
• Adults 18+ and children ages six months and older may participate.
• Children’s vaccines are available at all flu vaccination event sites.
• ONLY FREE THIS DAY – while supplies last.
• Bilingual staff & an ASL interpreter will be on site(s).
The flu vaccine is safe and effective. It can protect against common types of influenza and reduce the risk of the virus’s most serious symptoms and outcomes. Nationally, flu vaccination is estimated to have prevented approximately 10 million illnesses, 5 million medical visits, 180,000 hospitalizations, and 12,000 deaths during the 2024–2025 influenza season.
Pregnant people, infants, older adults, and individuals with chronic medical conditions face a higher risk of severe flu complications. Flu symptoms may include coughing, fatigue, fever, headache, muscle aches, sore throat, and a stuffy or runny nose.
For more information about precautions against respiratory viral illnesses, including influenza, visit the Tennessee Department of Health’s Respiratory Viral Illness webpage.

items.title: Informal work – which isn't covered by national labour laws, is not taxed and does not provide pension rights
items.content_text:
Informal work – which isn't covered by national labour laws, is not taxed and does not provide pension rights – is the norm for billions of workers. In some countries, economic growth has even coincided with rising informal employment.
 Across countries covered by a new #OECD report, 68% of workers are employed informally, with 16% of those informal workers being in highly paid jobs and possibly choosing to remain informal.
 Securing the Livelihoods of Informal Economy Workers in Times of Global Changes, launched today, provides insights on the diversity of informal work and how population ageing, the automation of work and environmental risks are reshaping the livelihoods of informal workers.
 Key findings:
 ➡️ Informal workers earn 44% less per hour than formal workers, limiting their ability to build financial security and withstand economic shocks.
 ➡️ One in three informal workers holds a job at high risk of being automated, nearly twice the rate among formal workers.
 ➡️ Informal workers are especially vulnerable to environmental degradation, particularly in developing countries where many depend on the natural environment for their livelihoods. More than 40% of informal workers face medium to high risks from floods and droughts, compared to less than 2% of formal workers. 
 As demographic shifts, technological change and environmental pressures increase risks to the livelihoods of informal workers, effective policies to strengthen their resilience are crucial for sustainable and inclusive economic growth.
 Find out more about what governments can do to support informal workers: https://brnw.ch/21x6bkv
 #OECDdevelopment
